en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Non-Proliferation, Concerning the Question on Inference.
3. The Question on the Forgetfulness of One Whose Taints are Exhausted “Venerable Nāgasena, is there forgetfulness of mindfulness for an Arahant?
“Great King, Arahants are free from forgetfulness of mindfulness; there is no forgetfulness of mindfulness for Arahants.”
“But, venerable sir, could an arahant fall into an offense?”—
“Yes, great king.”—
“On what basis?”

“By building a hut, O Great King, by acting as a go-between, by perceiving it as the right time when it is the wrong time, by perceiving that one has not been invited when one has been invited, and by perceiving food as ‘leftover’ when it is not leftover.
“Venerable Nāgasena, you say:
‘Those who commit an offense do so for two reasons: either out of disrespect or out of ignorance.’”
“But, venerable sir, does an arahant have disrespect when an arahant falls into an offense?
“Certainly not, Great King.
“If, venerable Nāgasena, an arahant falls into an offense, yet there is no disrespect on the part of an arahant, then it follows that an arahant has a lapse of mindfulness.”
“There is no lapse of mindfulness for an arahant, yet an arahant may commit an offense.
“In that case, venerable sir, convince me by means of a reason; what is the reason for this?
“Great king, there are these two kinds of defilements: those that are offenses by nature (*lokavajja*) and those that are offenses by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).”
What, Great King, is the offense against worldly convention?
The ten courses of unwholesome action—this is called the offense against worldly convention.
What is the offense against the rules of training?

Whatever in the world is unbecoming and unsuitable for recluses, yet blameless for householders—in that regard, the Blessed One lays down a training rule for his disciples, saying: "It is not to be transgressed as long as life lasts.
Eating at improper times, O Great King, is blameless in the world, but it is blameworthy in the teaching of the Conqueror.
"Great King, the destruction of living beings in a village is blameless in the world, yet it is a fault in the teaching of the Conqueror.
Great King, playing in the water is blameless in the world, yet it is a fault in the teaching of the Conqueror.
Thus, Great King, such things as these are faults in the teaching of the Conqueror; this is called a fault by rule."
An arahant whose taints are destroyed is incapable of transgressing what is wrong by way of the world.
As for that which is wrong by way of the rules of training, he might incur it through ignorance.
It is not within the scope of every arahant, Great King, to know everything; indeed, he does not possess the power to know all things.
"Great King, for an Arahant, even the names and clans of women and men are unknown; his path too is unknown upon this earth.
Great King, only one kind of Arahant might know liberation;
an Arahant possessing the six direct knowledges might know his own domain."
“O Great King, it is the Tathāgata alone, the All-Knowing One, who knows everything.
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
The third problem: On the Non-forgetfulness of those whose Taints are Destroyed.
